title: Brief madness
hookLine: anger is a brief madness, Seneca begins his book on it (On Anger 1.1)

cards: Anger has a face, and the angry person almost never sees it. Everyone else does. Seneca's brother Novatus once asked him to write about how anger might be calmed.
Seneca answered at length, and he opens not with a definition but with a mirror. Of all the passions, he says, anger is the most hideous and the most frenzied.
Then he borrows a short name for it from wise men who came before him.

teach.h: SOME WISE MEN: A BRIEF MADNESS.
teach.b: First, the phrase. Some wise men, Seneca writes, have called anger a brief madness, in Latin, brevis insania.
Like madness, it forgets decency, ignores friendship, won't listen to reason, and charges at what it wants even when the charge will hurt itself. The only difference is that it passes. Usually.
Seneca describes the angry face in close-up: eyes blazing, face flushing as the blood rushes up, lips trembling, teeth clenched, breath hissing, hands clapping together, feet stamping.
You can't tell, he says, whether this vice is more hateful or more ugly. He wants Novatus to see what everyone else sees.
Third, the body knows first. Seneca's list is all body. Long before we decide we're angry, the jaw has tightened, the heat has risen, the voice has gotten louder.
Those first signs are the useful ones, because they show up while there's still a gap before the words come out. Fourth, why this matters now.
Seneca spends the rest of the work on what to do about anger, but it starts with recognizing it. You can't step out of a madness you don't notice you're in.
A short madness is still a madness: a texted reply, a slammed door, a sentence you can't take back, all before the heat has cooled. Naming it as madness, while it's happening, is Seneca's first step.

how: Readers of Seneca's On Anger often learn their own first bodily signs of anger and name them as they happen, to catch anger before it speaks.

o: anger, which acts like madness but passes
a short burst of joy that clouds judgment
a sudden fever that comes with the summer heat

games.q: your brother asks how to calm anger. how does Seneca open his answer?
o: with a portrait of the angry face, and a name: brief madness.
by saying anger is sometimes useful.
games.why: he holds up a mirror first: blazing eyes, flushed face, and the old phrase, a brief madness.

practice: Bring back a recent moment of anger, a small one, and replay it slowly, following your body instead of the story: a hot face, a tight jaw, a quick breath, a jump in your voice.
Find your first sign, the one that shows up before anything else, then breathe out and let that part of you soften. That's your early warning.

wordCard.voice: Brief madness. Seneca's opening to On Anger: some wise men called anger a brief madness, deaf to reason, ugly in the face. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'a brief madness': the old phrase for anger that Seneca opens his book with.
